line: Hi, welcome. I'm Pilar Ochoa, I run the programs here at the hall. Are you here for the pantry, or just looking around?
Good, look around. Two things you should know. The coffee is free, and if you stand still too long I give you a job.
Saturday mornings, eight to eleven, side door. Bring ID if you have it. If you don't, come anyway. Sra. Reyes won't ask.
In the kitchen, just inside the door. The urn makes a noise like a train when it's ready. If it makes a different noise, come and get me.
Pantry on Saturdays, the roof raffle, the fiesta in the fall. And Tuesday nights, citizenship class, with the library across Grand.
choice3: That's a lot. I'll let you work.

line: For the test. A hundred civics questions, the interview, the reading part. Ruth Hale at the library sends the books, I send the people. Last month eleven passed.
choice3: Good for them. I should go.

line: The questions, not so much. The waiting room is hard. One lady called me from the bus home, crying, she was so happy. I couldn't understand a word.
choice3: That's lovely. I'll let you work.

line: Because the library is everybody's. People come here first because it feels like home. Then I walk them across Grand, and after a few Tuesdays the library feels like theirs too.
choice2: That's a good way to put it.

line: Slowly. Not everyone likes it. Don Aurelio worries the library takes our people and doesn't give them back. Ray thinks I'm too slow, that they should go straight to the Chamber.
I think they both love this place, and they should both come on a Tuesday and read the civics questions out loud. $ You too, if you want. We always need readers.
_thinks about it_ Somebody did it for me. I came from Puebla at sixteen, and a lady from this parish walked me to the high school office. That's all. It's not a long story.
I finished high school, I got a job, I came back here. Really, that's it. Ask me about the raffle instead, I talk much better about the raffle.
choice2: Another time. Good to meet you.

line: For the roof. It leaks over the kitchen door. First prize is a set of tires, and I have no idea who donated the tires and I'm afraid to ask.
Oh, hi. Sorry, I'm saving two chairs. Pilar Ochoa, from the parish hall on Grand. I'm here with a lady from the hall.
choice1: I'm {playerName}. Who are you here with?
choice3: I'd rather not chat right now.

line: Doña Carmen. She's in with Dr. Haddad. He talks fast and she nods, so I come along and say 'again, slower.'
By phone, yes, and it works. But on the phone she says yes to everything, to be polite. With me she says 'no, mija, that's not what happened.'
choice2: What else do you do at the hall?

line: Every other Thursday. The front desk knows me now. Last week the receptionist saved us the two chairs by the window.
choice2: Has it always been like that?
choice3: I'll let you get back to her.

line: No. When I started, the forms were only in English and Doña Carmen signed whatever they gave her. Now we read both versions together first. It's slow. Slow is fine.
She minds that I see her in the paper gown. Otherwise she brings me tamales. _glances at the door_ That's her. Come by the hall sometime.
Hi again. Doña Carmen again. We're early, which never helps.
She likes to be early, so the doctor is late, and then she worries they forgot her. I tell her nobody forgets Doña Carmen.
Her son drives her when he can. He drives a truck, so mostly it's me. He calls afterwards and asks me what the doctor said, not her.
choice3: I'll let you get back to her.

line: Because she tells him she's fine. She tells everyone she's fine. With the doctor she tells the truth, if I'm there and he talks slowly.
Morning, {playerName}. Grab a coffee, the urn is behaving today.
choice2: Are you the one in charge here?

line: Morning, {playerName}. Grab a coffee, the urn is behaving today.
choice2: Are you the one in charge here?

line: _laughs_ Somebody has to have the keys. The parish council says yes to most things I ask, and the priest says yes to the rest. So, yes. Ask me for anything.
choice1: Does everybody go along with that?

line: Two things I don't touch: Thursday nights, which belong to Don Aurelio and the Club, and the Club's money. I put his dance on the calendar first, before anybody asks. $ He thinks I'm giving the hall away to the library. I think I'm lending it. We get along fine.
Me? _laughs_ I run the programs. The hall runs on Don Aurelio. Nothing goes on the calendar without his nod.
choice2: How do you get his nod?

line: I ask him first, with a plate of pan dulce. If he says no, I hold it at the library instead and invite the Club anyway. $ [warm] He says the library takes our people. I say it lends them back. Nine years we've had that argument, and the pantry still opens every Saturday.
choice1: Sounds like you've found a way.

line: Raffle tickets. Four hundred sold, two hundred to go, and the roof doesn't care how tired I am.
Two things. You can take a book of tickets to work, or you can count these stubs with me for half an hour.
choice2: I'll take a book to work.

line: _counting_ Two-ninety, two-ninety-one. Don Aurelio bought forty tickets, by the way. He says it's for the roof, not for me. Same thing.
choice1: Is he not a fan of yours?
choice3: Here's my stack. I should go.

line: We disagree, that's different. His Club put a whole roof on a clinic in Jerez with no help from anybody. I want help from everybody. Both of us want roofs.
{playerName}, good. Do you have a minute? I want to ask you something.
The Tuesday class. I need someone to sit with the nervous ones. Not teaching. Just saying 'take your time' when they freeze on question forty.
Because you know both doors. You go from Spanish to English in the middle of a sentence and nobody gets lost, not even you. Most people are good in one room.
Not rare, just tired. It's two hours, seven to nine, in the library meeting room. Will you come one Tuesday and see?
Thursday, Ruth and I are doing a night at the library. Library cards, a lawyer for know-your-rights, pan dulce from Sra. Reyes's sister.
People who know both doors, standing at the door. Some will come because I asked them. They'll stay if they see a face they know.
Hi. Sorry, I'm counting chairs. We had fewer people on Tuesday.
Hi. Sorry, I'm a little distracted. Doña Carmen almost cancelled today. And on Tuesday the class had fewer people.
Four didn't come. One of them texted me. 'Better not to be on a list.'
choice3: I'm sorry. I'll let you work.

line: The sign-in sheet. The library asks for it, for their numbers. I keep it in my purse now, not on the table. $ [guarded] I don't know if that's smart or silly.
Legal aid on Fifth says first names are fine. So now it's first names. Ruth said okay without a single question. That's why I work with Ruth.

Two, maybe. I'll call them Monday, not to push, just so they know the chair is still there. $ [guarded] That's what this policy does. It divides a town into people who show up and people who stay home. I'm not letting it divide the hall.
{playerName}! I have good news, and I need to tell somebody who isn't on the parish council.
choice2: Congratulations. I have to run, though.

line: The city wants to fund the Tuesday class. A real teacher, books, maybe even chairs that don't wobble. $ That's what a president like this changes. The whole town gets to be the town, in every language. About time.
choice3: Good news. I'll let you celebrate.

line: Reports, every three months. Numbers, maybe names. Don Aurelio says city money comes with a leash.
choice3: I'll let you think it over.

line: He's not wrong that it comes with strings. I'll take the strings if they come with chairs. $ And I'll ask legal aid about the names first.
You're here so much I count you in the coffee now. Good.
choice2: Is that a lot of coffee?

line: {playerName}! Strange to see you somewhere without a coffee urn. At the hall I count you in the coffee now, you know.
choice1: Is that a lot of coffee?
choice2: I like it at the hall.

line: Twelve cups on a quiet night. Now, two things. You're welcome at the hall every day. And you should come with me on Tuesday, across Grand.
Because one day you'll need the library, or the clinic, or a city office, and I want you to already know the door. The hall isn't supposed to be the only room.
Ruth tells me you're at the library every week.
No, good. That's the whole idea. I just want you to come back across Grand sometimes and tell us what's going on over there.
The new hours, the programs, which librarian is patient. Half the people at the hall won't go until somebody they know has gone first.
Pilar is busy with a clipboard. "Hi."
choice1: Pilar, I'm sorry about last time.

line: Thank you. It's forgotten. Now, since you're here, hold these folders a second? I have more papers than hands.
Hi, {playerName}. Two minutes, sorry, I'm looking for the key to the storage room.
Folding chairs, the fiesta lights, and forty years of somebody's papers that nobody will let me throw out.
The parish's, the Club's, the softball team's. Every group in this building thinks the storage room is theirs, and they're all right. Ah, here's the key.
choice1: What else is going on this week?

line: Not now, the coffee urn is making the noise again. The noise means trouble.
